paragraphs: In the summer of Long’an’s fifth year, the Huai River grew yellower by the day.

Rain had fallen for half a month, soaking the embankments until their bases turned soft. At the old crossing on the southern bank floated the wreck of a bamboo raft, earthen jars, and the unclaimed carcass of an ox. Waves struck the mooring posts and splashed the guards’ faces with muddy water. Liu Yu had brought seven wounded soldiers and more than a dozen refugee families this far. Here the road ended.

The worst of the wounded lay in the cart with an arrow injury to his chest. The arrowhead had been removed ten days earlier, but the edges of the wound had blackened. Fever made him ramble. His surname was Cao; he was from Dantu, and his mother still lived in Jingkou. When he heard the day before that they meant to travel north, he gripped the side rail of the ox cart so tightly that no one could move him.
“If you cannot save me, Officer, leave me here,” he said weakly. “My mother can still burn offerings at my grave. Across the river she would not even know where to look for my bones.”

Liu Yu bent to feel his forehead. It was burning. He set a half-folded cloth, soaked in cool water, beneath the wounded man’s neck again and told a veteran to push the cart to higher ground first. Behind them the refugees stretched along the levee in a broken line. Children huddled inside their elders’ robes, their feet pale and swollen from standing in water. Some had fled Sun En along the southern roads the previous autumn, only to be driven onward again by armies collecting grain. Everything they could carry and still sell had already been sold along the way.

Feng Shi, a military clerk, handed Liu Yu an edict. It ordered strict precautions against refugees entering Qin territory without authorization and forbade the Northern Garrison from escorting them across on its own initiative. The seal was genuine, the characters plain enough. Liu had seen too many military orders in recent years. Some commanded him to pursue rebels, others to defend cities. The same troops might protect civilians today and be charged tomorrow for sheltering fugitives.
“If you send these seven wounded men across, how will you account for their places on the military rolls when Jiankang finds out?” Feng Shi asked.
“Write down seven men, sent for medical treatment.”
“What if the people on the northern bank will not send them back?”
“Let them survive tonight. We can ask about their return afterward.”

Feng was about to protest again when two short horn blasts rose from the river. A flat-bottomed boat put off from the timber stockade on the northern bank. At its bow stood a Qin officer in a rain cape, beside two physicians carrying baskets of medicine on their backs. As the boat approached, the officer raised a token to signal that neither bank should shoot.

“We can see your wounded,” he called across the water. “Whoever wishes to cross may do so, the sick first; weapons must be surrendered before boarding. The Qin camp has hot water and medicine. No one who does not wish to come will be detained.”
Feng Shi stepped forward, hand on sword. “What business is it of yours whether Jin soldiers live or die?”
The officer glanced at the ox cart. “If you have medicines yourselves, we shall go back.”

Feng’s hand stopped on the hilt. Liu pushed past him and asked how many empty cots were in the medical tents across the river. Twelve, the officer answered; they could clear six more by evening. There were medicines for the moment, but patients would have to be treated by severity. Liu asked whether the wounded, once healed, would be drafted directly into Qin’s army. The officer replied that frontier-camp medical regulations forbade the recruitment of captured wounded soldiers by compulsion. Disarmed patients would first have their identities checked. Those who wished to return south could leave under the existing agreements; those implicated in offenses would be examined separately.
“Then we shall go and see,” Liu Yu said.
“Officer!” Feng Shi exclaimed.
“You stay here. If I do not return in three double-hours, write that I entered Qin territory without authorization. You need not find softer words for it.”

He unfastened his sword and gave it to Feng, though he kept his official seal. When the wounded Cao Qi was lifted aboard, he began to struggle, clutching Liu’s sleeve and asking whether he would still be a Jin soldier once he reached the north. Liu tucked the dressing around his wound without making any grand promise. “If you wake and still want to return to Jingkou, I shall take you back,” he said.

It was too sweeping a promise, and Liu knew it. Midway across the river, the trees of the southern bank disappeared into mist. Looking back toward the people left behind, he suddenly felt how little right he had to promise any of them that one place must be better than another.

The northern bank held none of the tidy, spacious charitable shelters people described. Floodwater had already overtopped the first levee; mud lay ankle-deep beneath the thatched roofs, and the smell of medicines mingled with the sourness of spoiled grain. Three Qin soldiers were carrying sick men from the inner tents to dry ground, while others dug drainage trenches with spades. Two clerks stood at a half-wet wooden table. Their brushes slipped in their fingers, and every so often they had to hold their paper near a lamp to dry it.

When the seven wounded men reached the medical tent, the old physician examined their injuries without asking which standards they followed. When Cao Qi’s turn came, he unwound the blackened dressing and frowned. The dead flesh would have to be scraped away. Cao woke shouting that he would not let barbarians cut his flesh. Liu sat on the cot and held his shoulders, asking whether he had seen military physicians use knives at Jingkou. Cao nodded. It was only another knife, Liu told him; the first thing was to save his leg. Cao bit down on a wooden stick, veins standing out on the backs of his hands and sweat beading on his brow. Somehow he endured the cut.

After watching for a while, Liu walked to the registration table. An elderly woman held a child too sick to walk and begged the clerk to issue rations for two other ill members of her household. The clerk said that since they were not there, on what grounds could they receive food? He took up a wooden tally and circled the words “three persons,” his voice as flat as though he were asking how many bundles of firewood to distribute that day.
“They are in a boat shelter on the southern levee,” the woman said. “I carried this child here. There was no one to look after the other two.”
“Those who have not crossed the river cannot be entered on Qin registers.”
Liu intervened. “But you have taken down their boat’s passenger list, and the physicians said they would cross to collect people from the southern levee this afternoon.”
The clerk looked up. “Who are you?”
“A man who came in the same boat.”
“Then wait with your boat. Yours is not the only one.”

Several residents of the northern bank heard the argument and took the clerk’s side. Some had fallen behind in winter labor service and been pressed hard by the county. They had long resented seeing southerners arrive and receive grain and charcoal. An old farmer rolled up his sleeve to show an injury from building the levee. “Last year we worked the embankments until midnight. The medical tents never gave us this much medicine. Why should you get it?”

The old woman retreated two steps with the child in her arms. Liu did not shout at the farmer. Looking at the scar, he said that he too had seen men repairing levees in the south seized and sent off as soldiers. Had the farmer been paid everything he was owed? The old man stared, then cursed. “No! They still owe me four months.”

At that moment a blue-robed official came down from the levee, his boots thick with mud. He first ordered the woman’s sick child taken to a medical tent, then told the clerks to bring him the passenger list from the previous day and the register of patients. The clerk protested that the medical officer had not finished verifying it. The official folded the missing page and handed it to an attendant for checking, then ordered three days’ grain issued in advance rather than awaiting the completion of the case.
“If there is a shortfall in the county grain, I will enter it in the incidental-expense ledger under my own responsibility,” he said.
The clerk grew agitated. “My lord, there have been so many false claims in this camp of late…”
“Then arrest those who make false claims. You cannot declare everyone a fraud before they have even reached the table.”

He did not have the clerk bound on the spot. He ordered him to continue registration, complete the patients’ list before noon, and submit it that afternoon to a different granary clerk for review. The two young officials, neither willing to yield to the other, bowed their heads and carried off their respective account boards. The old farmer was still muttering about unpaid labor. The blue-robed man ordered his home village recorded and told the county office outside the camp to send over the register of wages owed. The farmer refused to give his name for fear the village head would retaliate. The official did not force him, but pointed out where he could bring a complaint.

Liu looked at the wooden board engraved with the route for filing grievances. Someone had burned such a board here the previous year. This one had been replaced, and fresh axe and chisel marks still showed around its edges.
“Do you handle every case this way?” Liu asked the man in blue.

“Every case? Hardly,” he said. “In the fortnight before you arrived, a camp clerk beat a young man from the south. The inquiry took eight days. His family stood outside my door every day. The soldiers accused me of favoring southerners; the southerners accused me of siding with Qin troops.”
“And in the end?”
“The soldier who struck him was flogged. His officer lost some pay. The scar is still on the young man’s face.”
“Aren’t you afraid they will burn the board again?”
“I am. The carpenter is waiting to carve another.”

Liu did not smile. He heard a messenger rush in to report that the tents nearest the water had flooded, and more than twenty households would have to move again. The blue-robed man tucked his robe into his belt and hurried down the slope. Several attendants called him “Your Highness of the Eastern Palace,” then stopped themselves. Liu looked at the man’s back and at last recognized Fu Hong. The Qin Crown Prince of rumor moved through the mud much like an ordinary county clerk carrying water for others.

Fu Hong turned. “Since Officer Liu has come, you might as well walk down with me. If you see only one medical tent and one ration table, you will not know how to describe this place when you return to Jiangnan.”
“You knew who I was?” Liu asked.
“You were among those who countersigned the receipt on the southern bank when twenty thousand shi of grain crossed the Huai last year.”
“Then you came here because of me?”
“This place has had three camp fires and more than ten disputes over land lately. I would have had to come even if you were not here.”

They walked north along the levee. The southerners’ temporary tents crowded together; beyond them lay the farm cottages of veteran soldiers and the local villages. The injured old farmer they had encountered was now arguing with several southerners over a stretch of riverbank. They had repaired its canal, but after the flood receded the county office had entered the land as uncultivated government property and granted it to registered guest households. The southerners also held land-allotment certificates with the county seal. Neither side lacked documents.

Fu Hong called for the county’s land survey maps. On the maps, the river ran in different places in successive years, gray and vermilion lines crossing and overlapping. The clerk pointed at a red line and called it the new embankment; the northerners produced the wage register from their canal repairs three years before. A widow among the southerners said that if she were moved once more, she and her two children would have to sleep on the road. The wheat she had planted was already sprouting. Uproot it once, and they faced another winter.

Fu Hong set both sets of documents on a mound of earth and ordered the transfer suspended. The government granary would cover the cost of the canal works and the southerners’ sowing for the time being. The boundary would be surveyed again in three days. No one praised him. The farmer pointed at him and cursed the county officials for failing to investigate sooner. The widow asked what she should do if, three days later, they still ruled that the land was not hers. Fu recorded every question without promising that she would be allowed to stay.
“You cannot decide it,” Liu Yu said.
“Not yet.”
“If both sides hold documents, someone will still lose the land in the end.”

Fu Hong turned the canal-wage register around and pointed to an altered entry. “First find whoever changed this line. If the government issued two certificates that contradict one another, then the government must pay compensation. We cannot let the two sides settle the matter with knives.”

As he spoke, a child stood beside them gripping the shaft of a hoe for his mother, his knuckles white with effort. Liu looked at the boy and felt he had seen those hands before. At the wharf in Xuyi, the child snatching up raw rice had clenched his fist in just that way, convinced anyone who came near meant to take his grain.

The rain grew heavier again that afternoon. Floodwater pushed one of the posts of the temporary dispensary askew. Several junior clerks called for the medicines to be moved, but no one dared first remove the wooden name boards hanging from the beams. They bore the patients’ names, and half those people were too weak even to stand. Fu Hong ordered the boards taken down and carried away in order. A young laborer helping with the medicine ran uphill with a chest on his shoulder. An old sword scar crossed it, and his accent was from the Kuaiji coast. When he heard an elderly southerner call for her son, he stopped and stood bewildered in the water for a moment.
“What is your name?” Liu called.
“Gu Asheng.”

Liu remembered him. When the coastal rebel army was defeated, he had personally ordered an inquiry into whether Gu Asheng had killed or looted. Later he heard that the man had crossed north, but had not expected to find him working in this camp. Gu said the inquiry had cleared him of killing while with the rebels. His old debts from the saltworks and the circumstances of his mother’s death still lacked proof, however. For now he could only work in the dispensary, saving a little money to send someone back to Shangyu to look for her grave.
“If you do not wish to stay, why not go back?”
“The south remembers that I served in a rebel army. The north remembers that I once was a rebel. Going back means passing two sets of checkpoints, and paying for two crossings.”

With that Gu Asheng ran toward the higher ground. Fu Hong watched him go but did not immediately order a favor granted. He merely entered the name in his pocket register and told someone to check Gu’s boat registration and the records from the salt case. Only then did Liu feel that the Qin Crown Prince’s little book might never be filled to its last page.

That night a section of the northern levee suddenly gave way. At first the water crept silently into a row of wooden sheds, then it drove dead branches against the fences and broke them apart. The guards hurried to shut the camp gates to prevent detainees escaping in the confusion, though more than ten patients remained in the medical shed. By the time Fu Hong arrived, a camp officer was clutching the heavy gate bar and refusing to release it. During an earlier camp fire, he said, soldiers who had stolen weapons had escaped into the reeds. Opening the gate now could bring another calamity.

Without a word Liu Yu leaped into the mud pit and pulled up the wooden bolt nearest the entrance. The camp officer flew into a rage and moved to seize him. As they were about to come to blows, Fu Hong ordered the side gate opened for the physicians first, while central-command troops established a separate checkpoint to search only for weapons. Three men carried each litter, and the patients moved slowly. People on the levee who had been cursing the southerners’ tents came down to help lift the stretchers when they saw the floodwater surge.

After carrying the third wounded person to safety, Gu Asheng suddenly shouted that someone remained behind: the southern widow who had argued over the land that day. She had gone back to the old shed for her child’s shoes and been trapped by the rising water. Liu borrowed a long rope, tied it around his waist, and waded across with two Qin soldiers. A slanting beam pinned the shed door. Liu braced his foot against the doorpost and together they raised the timber. The widow came out clutching the soaked shoes and immediately apologized. They were not valuable, she said, but her child’s old sores had only recently healed, and she could not make him walk barefoot again tomorrow.
Liu did not rebuke her. He saw the coarse, widely spaced stitches and soles worn halfway through. Even the words “Was it worth it?” seemed out of place.

It was nearly the third watch when the flood began to subside. The Crown Prince sat in a corner of a makeshift grain shed, allowing a physician to use a needle to extract a splinter that had broken off in his hand. Liu Yu returned from outside with water dripping from his clothes. The northern levee had held, he reported, but they would need at least two hundred laborers to strengthen it. Fu Hong said he had ordered the camps to hire labor by the day. Those who had come begging for grain could not be made to work without pay first. Liu looked at him. “And if there is not enough money in your treasury?”
Fu Hong gave a wry smile. “Then we move money we shall have to replace next year. It is easier to owe a debt than to bury people tonight.”

For a time neither spoke. The wind no longer carried rain across the river. Someone in the dispensary was singing softly in an accent from Jiangnan. Across the water a Jin patrol lamp appeared and disappeared, as faint as a firefly deep among distant trees.

By daylight Cao Qi’s fever had broken, though he still could not be moved. Many among the hundred-odd remaining refugees decided to stay; several households still wished to return. A carpenter from Dantu handed back the government’s wooden land-allotment token, explaining that his family graves were in Jiangnan and he could not bear to leave his aged father there alone. One woman said her son had finally eaten three meals of hot porridge. She would sooner accept three years of guest registration than set foot on the southward road again.

Liu listened to each household without deciding for them. He wrote Cao Qi’s name and condition on a sheet he carried and instructed the physician on the northern bank to send a message to Jingkou by military relay if the wound worsened. Fu Hong issued him a crossing permit allowing him to return under the agreement within three days, without further questioning by Qin soldiers.

Before Liu boarded, Fu Hong invited him to stay in the north. He offered no noble title or rank, saying only that Liu’s military experience could be put to use in civil administration or camp affairs if he wished. Liu shook his head.
“Of those who came with me, some will stay and some will go back,” he said. “Each has a home to think of. So do I.”
“The Jin court?”
“No.”

Fu Hong did not ask again. Seeing Liu fasten his two wet shoes, fresh blisters rubbed into his heels, he ordered a pair of dry boots brought. Liu accepted without protest, but gave his old boots to the young dispensary worker from Kuaiji. Gu Asheng stood at the crossing holding them for a long time. Only after the boat had pulled away did he lower his head and pick the clots of mud from their soles one by one.

That night someone in the medical shed had bound an injury with old red cloth from an army uniform. Seeing Gu enter, he casually called him “one of the Celestial Master’s men.” Gu Asheng did not grow angry. He opened his medicine pouch and gave the man clean hemp cloth, waiting until the wound was dressed before saying that while his mother had lived she feared most of all that red cloth would catch the soldiers’ eyes. The other man watched him and quietly asked whether what happened in those days would still be investigated. Gu said yes: the people at the county office were still waiting for him to return and seek an answer.

When the skiff reached midstream, Liu Yu looked back at the northern bank. The dispensary was being rebuilt on higher ground; camp soldiers and refugees were digging a new drainage channel together. The old farmer and southern widow who had disputed the land were still arguing across the watercourse. Carrying patients together the night before had not made them forget their grievances.

He had once hoped the north would prove wholly cruel and oppressive, so that he could tell the soldiers of Jiangnan without hesitation: the people beyond this river have nothing worth learning from. What he saw instead were people who could bully others, shirk labor, falsify accounts, and quarrel, just as people did in the south, and people who, after dark, would help carry a stranger’s sickbed. He had no intention of speaking on Qin’s behalf, nor would one night’s rescue persuade him to surrender Jiangnan.

On the southern bank Feng Shi was waiting impatiently. As Liu stepped ashore, Feng first asked how many Jin soldiers the Qin had kept, and then whether the Crown Prince had tempted him with office and rank. Liu handed over the crossing permit and told him to record it exactly. When Feng turned to Cao Qi’s entry and saw the medical camp, the injury, and the expected date of return all listed there, he could find no words for a while.
“What do we do next?” he asked.

Liu looked toward Jingkou. The rain had not ceased in the south. Several official roads had vanished into the watery haze. Liu Laozhi’s standards still flew over Jingkou, but who would command them next year was uncertain. Huan Xuan’s power had traveled downriver from Jingzhou, Jiankang issued new edicts day after day, and villages along the way were forced to feed each army that arrived.
“Back to camp,” Liu Yu said. “First reconcile the compensation owed to the wounded and the wages owed to the civilian laborers.”
“And then?”
“Make the men who would carry patients with us tonight willing to defend the city beside us tomorrow.”
Feng glanced at him. “Defend a city with an account book?”

Liu Yu drew the sheet of names from his wet robe, folded it twice, and slipped it back against his chest. He gave no answer. Rain dragged at the Jin banner on the bank; its pole leaned toward Jiangnan. Liu Yu righted it himself before leading his men onto the muddy road.
